subject: Zephyrus pilot: provisioning runway, tokens/sec estimates & SLO headroom
messages:
From: Maya R. <maya@zephyrus.ai>

Cc: eng@zephyrus.ai

Subject: Pilot sizing ask: 95p latency target + tokens/sec forecast

Hi Grace / Ben —

Thanks again for the call today. As we discussed, the pilot will be chat-driven (assistant + user history), average user prompt ~28 tokens, average assistant reply ~140 tokens, with an expected peak of ~1.8k concurrent active users during our initial marketing window. Zephyrus wants 95th-percentile latency for chat completions <= 220ms (end-to-end) to preserve product UX.

Two asks to make progress on contract and Dedicated sizing:
- Can Redwood provide a tokens/sec (TPS) model that maps our expected concurrency and typical convo lengths to GPU SKUs and p95 latency estimates? We care about realistic headroom for cold starts and session KV caching.
- We attached a quick spreadsheet (zephyrus_mtp_estimates.xlsx) with per-session assumptions. Please call out any obvious missing inputs.

We also need to know if a single Dedicated slab can satisfy the pilot or whether you recommend a primary+fallback approach (smaller cheaper model for spikes).

Goal: get a recommended provisioning plan and a short paragraph we can include in our internal procurement review by Thurs 9/17.

Thanks — happy to hop on another quick call if helpful.

—Maya
Maya R., Head of Platform
Zephyrus AI

From: grace_oconnor <grace@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Pilot sizing ask: 95p latency target + tokens/sec forecast

Maya — thanks for the clear ask and the sheet (reviewed). High level answer up front: we can meet a 95p <= 220ms for the pilot with a dedicated slab sized to the expected concurrent active users if we (a) target a quantized LLM variant with warmed KV cache for session context, (b) reserve a 20-30% burst headroom for cold starts and marketing spikes, and (c) enable prefix caching + autoscale burst.

Next steps from Redwood: Ben + Karthik will produce a short run-rate model (tokens/sec by SKU, p95 latency estimate, and recommended slab config) and a recommendation for primary/fallback paths. I pulled a few quick back-of-envelope numbers into the reply below to set expectations.

Key assumptions I used from your sheet: average request total tokens = 168 (28 user prompt + 140 assistant), average token generation cost environment ~= our rllm-gpu-1 24GB quantized runtime.

Quick back-of-envelope:
- Per-session throughput baseline: if 1 request ~168 tokens and model emits at ~300 tokens/sec on a single rllm-gpu-1 quantized, then a single GPU can support ~1.8 reqs/sec (~302 tokens/sec / 168 tokens).
- For 1.8k concurrent active users assuming an average think time that maps to 0.02 reqs/sec per active user (i.e., sessions generate ~1 request every 50s), aggregate concurrency here means ~36 reqs/sec (1.8k * 0.02).
- Tokens/sec needed = 36 reqs/sec * 168 tokens = ~6,048 tokens/sec.

Rough slab mapping:
- If each rllm-gpu-1 provides ~300 tokens/sec, you'd need ~21 GPUs raw (6,048 / 300 = 20.16). With 25% SLO headroom for spikes and cold tails, that's ~26 GPUs.
- If we use a denser sku (rllm-gpu-4 with multi-instance packing + faster kernels -> ~1,200 tokens/sec effective), you can fit on ~6 GPUs raw, or ~8 with 25% headroom.

Ben / Karthik — can you validate these runtime numbers and produce a small table with quantized vs fp16 variants, expected p95 token latency impact, and a recommended slab (primary + fallback) for the pilot? Maya: we'll aim to get that to you by end of day Wed 9/16 so you have something for the Thurs internal review.

Cheers,
Grace
Grace O'Connor
Director, Enterprise Sales — Redwood Inference

On Wed, Sep 15, 2026 at 10:03 AM grace_oconnor <grace@redwood.com> wrote:
> Ben / Karthik — can you validate these runtime numbers and produce a small table with quantized vs fp16 variants, expected p95 token latency impact, and a recommended slab (primary + fallback) for the pilot?

Quick validation and concrete table here (summary only — attaching micro-sim):

Assumptions we validated from infra bench:
- Model footprint: baseline open-llm-compat v1.2 quantized 4-bit (Q4) running on rllm-gpu-1: steady-state generation ~320 tokens/sec single-stream; p95 per-token gen latency ~3ms per token under warm KV cache.
- rllm-gpu-4 (packed multi-instance) effective aggregate ~1,150 tokens/sec with similar per-token p95 when batching is efficient.
- Cold start penalty: first token generation can add 60-90ms while kernels settle and KV warms; effective for un-cached sessions.

Concrete numbers (pilot workload = 36 reqs/sec, 168 tokens each -> 6,048 tokens/sec):
- Option A: Quantized Q4 on rllm-gpu-4: need 6 GPUs raw (6,048 / 1,150 = 5.26). With 30% buffer for marketing spikes and cold tails -> 8 GPUs. Estimated p95 end-to-end (model-only) ~140-170ms plus 20-40ms network/ingress -> ~180-210ms, meets your 220ms target with a small margin.
- Option B: Q4 on rllm-gpu-1 (single-instance conservative): need 19-21 GPUs raw, 25-28 with buffer. Estimated p95 end-to-end ~200-240ms (risky at 220ms target) unless we use aggressive KV warm strategies and autoscale to reduce cold fractions.
- Option C: FP16 on rllm-gpu-4 (higher mem, slightly slower kernels): need 9-10 GPUs with 25% buffer; p95 ~190-230ms.

Recommendation for pilot: Option A (Q4 on rllm-gpu-4) as primary slab (8 GPUs) + a very small fallback pool (2 x rllm-gpu-1 running a cheaper trimmed model - cheaper model handles sudden overshoot with higher latency but keeps requests served). This combination balances cost and SLO.

Operational notes to include in the runbook:
- Enable prefix & KV caching per active session for the marketing window; warm top 20% of sessions when possible.
- Autoscale policy: aggressive small-step scale every 30s for sustained rise, instant burst fallback to fallback pool for short spikes.
- Instrument: track cold-fraction metric and p95-by-cold-flag.

I'll attach the micro-sim and a short cost delta between Option A vs Option B.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Senior Infra Engineer — Redwood Inference
